title: Days, months, and dates
title_target: আজ কী বার? — aj ki bar?
goal: Name the days, months, and dates — and discover that Bengali weekday names come from the same list of seven planets as English Sunday, Monday, and Saturday.
bekal: name the seven days and recognize their Sanskrit roots
give months and dates with পয়লা, দোসরা, তেসরা
use কাল and পরশু, each of which points in two directions
know when the weekend falls in Bangladesh and in West Bengal

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — Planning the week
dialogs.intro: Ani and Rahim sit on the veranda making plans. Listen to the names of the days: they follow the same seven planets that gave English *Sunday*, *Monday*, and *Saturday*.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Today is Wednesday. Tomorrow is Thursday.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Budhbar! In Java we call it Buda.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Really? Then what about Monday? Friday?

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Soma and Sukra! Same names, same planets.
lines.literal: soma — and — sukra! same — name, same — planet.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Amazing! Well, Friday is our day off.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: In Bangladesh it's Friday and Saturday. In Kolkata it's Sunday.
lines.literal: bangladesh-in — Friday — and — Saturday. kolkata-in — Sunday.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I see. And when is Pohela Boishakh?

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: April fourteenth. Bengali New Year. The biggest festival.
lines.literal: fourteenth — april. bengali — new-year. most — big — festival.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I'll still be here then! What should I wear?
lines.literal: I — then — will-stay — you-know! what — to-wear — becomes?

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Red and white. Everyone wears them. We'll take you along too.
lines.literal: red — and — white. everyone — wears. you(polite)-too — taking — will-go.

notes: **Bengali weekday names follow the same seven heavenly bodies as the European week.** Each day is named for a planet in Sanskrit: রবি (sun) → *Sunday*, সোম (moon) → *Monday*, মঙ্গল (Mars) → French *mardi*, বুধ (Mercury) → *mercredi*, বৃহস্পতি (Jupiter) → *jeudi*, শুক্র (Venus) → *vendredi*, শনি (Saturn) → *Saturday*. ⚠️ It's no coincidence but a shared ancient system; match each day to its planet and the seven names stick quickly. (Ani knows them from the Javanese–Balinese calendar, which uses the same Sanskrit names.)

**All day names end in -বার** *bar*, meaning “day”. So “what day?” is **আজ কী বার?** — literally “today what day?”. ⚠️ In fast speech people often drop -বার: শুক্র আর শনি ছুটি (Friday and Saturday are off).

⚠️ **The weekend falls on different days on each side of the border.** In **Bangladesh**, the weekly days off are **Friday and Saturday**, since Friday is the day of congregational prayer. In **West Bengal (India)**, the day off is **Sunday**. If you schedule across the border — or email a Dhaka office on a Friday — the difference is real.

⚠️ **কাল means both yesterday and tomorrow — the verb decides.** কাল এসেছি = “I came yesterday”. কাল যাব = “I'll go tomorrow”. Bengali sees both as “the day next to today” and leaves the direction to the verb form. For clarity there are **গতকাল** (yesterday) and **আগামীকাল** (tomorrow), but in everyday talk people rarely use them.

⚠️ **পরশু also points both ways:** “the day after tomorrow” and “the day before yesterday”. পরশু আসব = I'll come the day after tomorrow; পরশু এসেছিলাম = I came the day before yesterday. Again, the verb decides. English needs two long phrases; Bengali uses one word and lets grammar do the work.

**Dates use ordinal forms, and the first four are irregular.** ১ **পয়লা** *pôyla*, ২ **দোসরা** *dosra*, ৩ **তেসরা** *tésra*, ৪ **চৌঠা** *chouTha* — much like English *first, second, third*. From the 5th on, just add **-ই** to the number: পাঁচই, ছউই, সাতই, দশই, চৌদ্দই. From the 20th on, the pattern becomes **-এ**: বাইশে, পঁচিশে.

**Bengal uses two calendars at once.** The Gregorian calendar is used for official business, but the Bangla calendar — with its own twelve months: বৈশাখ, জ্যৈষ্ঠ, আষাঢ়, শ্রাবণ, ভাদ্র, আশ্বিন, কার্তিক, অগ্রহায়ণ, পৌষ, মাঘ, ফাল্গুন, চৈত্র — lives on in festivals, farming, and poetry. ⚠️ **পহেলা বৈশাখ**, the first day of Boishakh (April 14), is Bengali New Year, the biggest festival, celebrated together by Muslims and Hindus on both sides of the border.

grammars.title: The seven days — সাত বার
after: **বৃহস্পতিবার is the longest word you'll meet in this unit** — six syllables. The good news: Bengalis themselves often shorten it to **বেস্পতিবার** *bèspôtibar* in casual speech.

grammars.title: Months, dates, and units of time
after: **সপ্তাহ comes from সপ্ত — “seven” — a cousin of Latin *septem* and English *seven*.** Once you see it, the word stops feeling foreign: it literally means “a set of seven”.
⚠️ **কবে asks which day; কখন asks what time.** আপনি কবে আসবেন? (what day are you coming?) versus আপনি কখন আসবেন? (what time are you coming?). English uses “when” for both.

blocks.title: Three festivals you should know
items: **পহেলা বৈশাখ** *pôhéla boishakh* — Bengali New Year, April 14. Everyone wears red and white, the streets fill with processions, and the must-have breakfast is panta bhat — rice soaked overnight. ⚠️ It's a festival of **language and culture**, not religion, celebrated together by Muslims and Hindus.

**একুশে ফেব্রুয়ারি** *ékushé phèbruari* — February 21, International Mother Language Day. People walk barefoot to the Shohid Minar monument carrying flowers, remembering the students killed in 1952. ⚠️ The day is very quiet and deeply respected; dress simply.
**দুর্গাপূজা** *durgapuja* (September–October) and **ঈদ** *id* — the two great religious festivals. A safe greeting for both: **শুভেচ্ছা** *shubhéchchha* (best wishes) or **ঈদ মোবারক**.

blocks.text: One expression you'll hear often that no dictionary prepares you for: **আজকাল** *ajkal* — literally “today-tomorrow”, meaning “these days”. Bengali often builds new words by joining two related or opposite words: আসা-যাওয়া (coming-going, meaning people's comings and goings), খাওয়া-দাওয়া (eating-giving, meaning a meal or feast), লেখাপড়া (writing-reading, meaning education). ⚠️ When you hear two words you know joined together, the meaning is almost always broader than the sum of the two.

answers: আজ কী বার? — শুক্রবার আমার ছুটি। — আমি এক সপ্তাহ থাকব। — পরশু দেখা হবে। — আজ কত তারিখ?
আজ কী বার? — কাল বৃহস্পতিবার। — শুক্রবার আমার ছুটি। — আপনি কবে আসবেন? — আমি এক মাস থাকব। — আজ চৌদ্দই এপ্রিল।
